frontmatter_description: Diagnose whether a character has the background knowledge needed to interpret information, without confusing it with perception, memory, or factual belief.
title: Knowledge Boundary
use_when: Use when the question is whether the character has enough professional, cultural, experiential, or conceptual background to understand what was said, shown, or implied.
Use when the key issue is comprehension blocked by missing background knowledge, not by not seeing, not remembering, or holding a false belief.
Use when one person would understand a reference, term, custom, or concept and another would not because of different prior knowledge.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the main issue is whether the character noticed, heard, saw, or otherwise perceived the information.
Do not use when the main issue is whether the character remembers, forgets, or misremembers something they previously knew.
Do not use when the main issue is what the character believes is true or false about the world; route to belief or false-belief skills instead.
Do not use when the question is about intention, emotion, persuasion, or social etiquette unless the decisive barrier is background competence itself.
decision_variable: whether the character has the background required to interpret the information
trigger_checklist: Is the barrier missing training, expertise, culture, experience, or conceptual familiarity?
Would the character still fail to understand even if they clearly perceived the information?
Is the contrast between informed and uninformed listener the key diagnostic split?
Does the scene ask about comprehension of jargon, reference, custom, or domain-specific meaning?
workflow: Identify the exact information the character must interpret.
Ask what background knowledge is required to make sense of it.
Check whether the character has that background.
Infer understanding, partial understanding, or misunderstanding from that knowledge gap.
Do not infer lack of perception, memory, or false belief unless the scene explicitly asks for those.

special_case.title: Hears the words but lacks the key
special_case.rule: If the character perceives the message but cannot decode its meaning because they lack the needed background, this is still Knowledge Boundary.

worked_example.scene: A nurse tells a patient that the test result is "benign." The patient hears the word clearly but does not know its medical meaning.
worked_example.question: Does the patient understand what the nurse means?
worked_example.answer_logic: Yes, this is a knowledge boundary case: perception is intact, but the patient lacks the medical background needed to interpret the term.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to micro-09 if the issue is whether the character once learned it, now retains it, or has forgotten it.
Exit to micro-11 or micro-12 if the issue is what the character thinks is true, not whether they have the background to interpret it.
Exit to micro-05 if the issue is whether the character saw, heard, or noticed the cue at all.
Stop when the diagnostic is complete and the task moves to emotion, intention, or action prediction.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when the scene hinges on whether a person can correctly interpret information because of missing background knowledge, expertise, or cultural context.
hard_boundary: Not perception: the person may have clearly heard or seen the information.
Not memory: the person may once have known it or never learned it at all.
Not belief truth status: the issue is comprehension, not whether the belief matches reality.
Not social intention: do not use unless interpretation depends specifically on background competence.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not treat every misunderstanding as false belief.
Do not infer ignorance from silence, confusion, or surprise unless the missing background is explicit.
Do not collapse domain expertise into general intelligence.
Do not use this for word meaning alone if the scene is actually about belief, deception, or memory.
common_failure_modes: Confusing not knowing a term with not believing a fact.
Choosing memory when the character never had the relevant background in the first place.
Choosing perception when the character saw the cue but lacked the context to decode it.
Overgeneralizing from one narrow technical example to all comprehension problems.

minimal_pair.case: A mechanic and a six-year-old both clearly see the same dashboard warning light; the mechanic explains it, the child cannot.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Perception is identical, so the deciding variable is background knowledge needed to interpret the cue.

minimal_pair.case: The same six-year-old once had the warning light explained to them but cannot recall what it meant a year later.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Near miss: the child once had the relevant background, so the deciding variable is retention rather than competence; route to Memory, Forgetting, and Misremembering.

boundary_stress_test: The character heard the sentence perfectly, but cannot explain what it means.
The character saw the symbol, but lacks the training to decode it.
The character is confused because the reference depends on local culture or profession, not because they forgot it.
references.generalization_note: This unit generalizes to any prior-knowledge gap that blocks interpretation, including professional, cultural, experiential, and conceptual background.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: The character perceives the information but lacks the background needed to understand it.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The character once knew it but now cannot recall it.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The character misunderstands because they saw or heard nothing important.

notes: Keep the boundary strict: background competence only.
Treat this as a diagnostic unit for comprehension gaps, not a broad misunderstanding skill.
When in doubt between knowledge boundary and belief, ask whether the question is about understanding the information or accepting it as true.
core_question: Determine whether a character has the background knowledge needed to understand information
